Geometry | Quarter 2 | Unit 4: Quadrilaterals and Polygons

The Chainring Polygon

Where do 32 teeth sit?

Duration
50 minutes
Grade level
Grades 9–10
Topic
Regular Polygons
Standards
HSG-CO.A.3, HSG-MG.A.1, HSG-C.A.3

Students name and classify polygons, find interior, exterior and central angles of regular polygons, and find their areas with the apothem, using a chainring as a regular polygon.

2Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  • Name polygons and classify them as regular or irregular, convex or concave.
  • Find the interior, exterior and central angles of a regular polygon.
  • Find the area of a regular polygon using A = 12aP.
  • Model a chainring as a regular polygon.

3Essential question

Why do the teeth of a chainring sit exactly at the corners of a regular polygon?

5MTB connection

A chainring’s teeth are evenly spaced around a circle, so they sit at the vertices of a regular polygon. The chain’s links, all the same length, sit on that polygon as the chain wraps.

The more teeth, the closer the polygon is to a circle. Engineers even talk about “chordal action”: the chain rising and falling slightly because it rides a polygon, not a true circle.

The mathOn the trail
Regular n-gonA chainring or cog with n teeth
Central angleAngle between neighbouring teeth
Side lengthThe chain pitch (12.7 mm, half an inch)
More sidesA smoother, rounder ring

MTB Problem-Based Exercise

Chainring Geometry

Model chainrings and cogs as regular polygons and compute their angles and perimeters.

You’ll need: A real chainring or cog (optional); Calculator; Chain pitch: 12.7 mm
